query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges under service-relevant conditions because stress- and temperature-driven short-range ordering at grain boundaries leads to the formation of nanoscale clusters that undermine boundary cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase, compositionally complex HEA with a stable microstructure (i.e., no pre-existing grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitates).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the thermal hold time at intermediate temperatures and the strain rate during pre-deformation to enhance or suppress the kinetics of short-range ordering (nanoclustering) at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant regimes characterized by intermediate temperatures (e.g., conditions where thermal activation is sufficient for local atomic rearrangements but not full phase separation) combined with controlled mechanical loading at varied strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range atomic ordering (nanoclustering) occurring at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under combined thermal and mechanical loading, atoms near grain boundaries rearrange into ordered nanoclusters. This localized ordering reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries, making them more susceptible to crack initiation and propagation, thereby leading to brittle fracture even though the bulk alloy remains as a single-phase solid solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA samples subjected to extended intermediate-temperature aging and low strain rate pre-deformation (conditions favoring ordering) will exhibit detectable nanoclusters at grain boundaries and show a reduction in toughness (lower fracture toughness, earlier crack initiation) compared to a baseline sample with minimal aging and higher strain rate pre-deformation.
generation.baseline: Samples maintained in the as-homogenized, single-phase condition with minimal thermal aging and rapid deformation to inhibit grain-boundary short-range ordering.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative under service conditions where temperature and strain rate allow significant short-range ordering; at very high temperatures (where complete phase changes might occur) or extremely high strain rates (insufficient time for ordering), the effect may not manifest as predicted.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of grain-boundary ordering, the quantitative reduction in toughness, and the precise interplay of thermal and mechanical activation remain uncertain and require further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of identical single-phase HEA specimens. For one set, apply controlled thermal aging at an intermediate temperature combined with a low strain rate pre-deformation to promote grain-boundary ordering. For the control set, apply rapid deformation with minimal thermal aging to inhibit ordering. Use high-resolution TEM and grain-boundary spectroscopy (EDS/EELS) to examine the extent of short-range ordering. Perform fracture toughness tests (e.g., measuring KJIc) and stress–strain experiments to correlate mechanical performance with the observed microstructural changes.
measurements: High-resolution TEM imaging and EDS/EELS mapping of grain-boundary regions for nanocluster identification
Fracture toughness (KJIc) and crack propagation tests
Stress–strain behavior under controlled loading conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention promoting grain-boundary ordering does not produce a statistically significant increase in nanoclustering (as seen by microscopy and spectroscopy) and does not correlate with a measurable reduction in toughness compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The ductility loss in metals and alloys can be related to the segregation of impurity elements at GBs (, ) and the absorption of hydrogen or helium (), which weaken GB strength and promote crack initiation at GBs, and the precipitation of second phases (intermetallic compounds, carbides, nitrides, oxides, etc.) at GBs (, ), which causes high stress/strain concentration due to the incompatibility of elastic and plastic deformation between particles and matrix. In contrast to carbides and nitrides, intermetallic compound–induced embrittlement at room temperature can be relieved at high temperatures because plastic codeformation between these compounds and the matrix can reduce stress concentration and, thus, delay crack initiation (). decision.trend: Early HEA studies showed that these alloys can avoid the classic pitfalls of conventional grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation, thereby maintaining high strength–ductility and thermal stability. Later work, notably PMC6897545, indicated that even in single‐phase high-entropy systems ductility loss may occur via grain-boundary nanoclustering. The research trajectory moved from designing compositionally complex alloys with intrinsically stable microstructures to detecting subtle grain-boundary phenomena—such as localized elemental clustering—that correlate with a transition toward brittle behavior. However, while the role of nanoclustering has been documented, the precise mechanistic connection (for example, whether stress or thermal activation drives a short‐range ordering at grain boundaries that undermines cohesion) remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how an initially uniform, compositionally complex HEA transitions to brittle behavior without the classic segregation and intermetallic phases seen in conventional alloys. In particular, the potential for stress- or temperature-induced short-range ordering or subtle nanochemical redistribution at grain boundaries to trigger embrittlement has not been decisively tested under service-relevant conditions.
decision.lever: Systematically vary thermal hold times and strain rates to control the kinetics of short-range ordering at grain boundaries. This experiment would involve comparing a baseline HEA sample with samples subjected to controlled thermal-aging and mechanical pre-deformation designed to promote or inhibit subtle local ordering, while using in situ advanced microscopy and spectroscopy to monitor grain-boundary chemistry and fracture behavior.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend from studies showing nanoclustering-related ductility loss in HEAs, and it distinguishes the hypothesized mechanism from conventional segregation paradigms by testing the role of stress-activated short-range ordering. The planned controlled comparison under service and loading regimes (intermediate temperatures and varied strain rates) provides a decisive means to falsify the hypothesis if such ordering is not correlated with a reduction of toughness.
